title: Building a Skyscraper
objective: After this level you can describe the steps from foundation to top.
summary: A skyscraper starts with a pit and piles to bedrock; a concrete core climbs first, the steel frame follows, floors go on steel decking, and the outer wall and fit-out overlap.

cards.headline: A skyscraper starts by going down.
cards.body: Before anything rises, builders dig a pit to hold the foundation. Then the tower grows in layers, and several of those layers are being built at the same time. Here's the order, from the bottom up.

cards.headline: Down to rock
cards.body: Piles, which are vertical beams, are sunk through the soil until they're embedded in the bedrock. That's where Level 2's load path ends. A continuous path carries the loads from the roof down through the building to the foundation, and into the ground that holds it all up. For a piled tower, that ground is rock.

cards.headline: The core goes first
cards.body: Many towers are built core-first. A concrete core, holding the stairways, elevators and utility risers, is cast inside a self-climbing form: a giant mold that climbs as the core rises. The steel framing follows once the forms have climbed clear. Here's an analogy: the spine grows first, and the rest of the skeleton catches up.

cards.headline: Frame, floor, skin
cards.body: Cranes lift each steel beam into place, where skilled workers bolt or weld it. Thin corrugated steel decking goes down on the beams, and about 5 to 10 cm of concrete is poured on top to make a floor. Panels of glass, metal or stone are bolted to the frame as the outer wall, then come wiring, pipes and elevators. All of it overlaps: frame at the top, walls and wiring lower down.

cards.headline: Skyscraper: built
learned: Dig a pit; sink piles to bedrock
Core-first: a concrete core climbs in a self-climbing form
Beams by crane; floors of steel decking and concrete
Outer wall and fit-out follow; phases overlap

questions.prompt: How is a floor usually made on a skyscraper's steel beams?

options.label: Thick stone slabs laid across the beams
options.rationale: Stone is too heavy; the floor is decking and concrete.

options.label: Wooden planks nailed to the beams
options.rationale: The floor is steel decking with concrete on top.

options.label: Glass panels bolted to the beams
options.rationale: Glass goes on the outer wall, not the floor.

options.label: Corrugated steel decking with concrete poured on top

questions.explanation: Steel decking is laid on the beams and about 5 to 10 cm of concrete is poured on it to complete the floor.

questions.prompt: In core-first construction, what is the self-climbing form?

options.label: A crane that lifts steel beams to the top
options.rationale: Cranes lift beams; the form shapes the concrete core.

options.label: A giant mold the concrete core is cast in, climbing as it rises
A temporary elevator for the workers
options.rationale: The core will hold elevators; the form is the mold.

options.label: A glass panel system for the outer wall
options.rationale: That's the curtain wall, added later.

questions.explanation: The core is cast in a self-climbing form, a giant mold, and the steel framing follows once it climbs clear.

questions.prompt: Level 2's load path ends in the ground. Where does a piled skyscraper's load path end?

options.label: In the bedrock, where the piles are embedded
At the top of the concrete core
options.rationale: The core carries loads down; the path ends below.

options.label: In the outer glass wall
options.rationale: The curtain wall holds only itself.

options.label: In the basement floor slab
options.rationale: The piles carry the load on down into bedrock.

questions.explanation: Piles are sunk through the soil until embedded in bedrock, where the tower's load path ends.
